image_description: A close-up, side-view of a male duck (drake) floating on water. The image focuses on the rear half of the bird, showing detailed plumage textures, the characteristic curled tail feathers, and the blue speculum patch on the wing. The head is partially visible on the far left, showing a chestnut color, while the bill and eyes are largely out of frame or obscured.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Most distinctive feature is the broad, flat bill adapted for filter-feeding; bill is dark grey to yellow-green.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The head is positioned at the extreme left edge of the frame and is significantly cropped. The bill is not visible in the provided image.
The eye is located on the cropped portion of the head and is not visible.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body is stocky and compact, streamlined and buoyant with dense waterproof plumage.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible torso exhibits a streamlined, buoyant shape sitting low in the water. The plumage appears dense and textured, consistent with waterproof feathers.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Breeding plumage is typically more colorful than female: common patterns include iridescent green head with white neck ring and grey body (mallard), or chestnut head with grey body.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The visible portion of the head/neck shows chestnut coloring, and the body features complex grey/brown patterning with a distinct blue and white wing patch (speculum), which is characteristic of male dabbling ducks like the Mallard or Gadwall.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Legs are short and set far back on the body with webbed feet (three forward toes connected by webbing).
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The legs and feet are submerged beneath the water line and are completely occluded.
The folded wing is clearly visible on the back, showing the correct anatomical position and the distinctive blue speculum patch bordered by white bars.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Tail is short with curled central tail feathers (drake feathers) in many species.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The tail feathers are clearly visible and exhibit the characteristic upward curl typical of drakes.
